title: The Frogs' Complaint Against the Sun
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: Once upon a time the Sun was about to take to himself a wife. The Frogs in terror all raised their voices to the skies, and Jupiter, disturbed by the noise, asked them what they were croaking about. They replied, "The Sun is bad enough even while he is single, drying up our marshes with his heat as he does. But what will become of us if he marries and begets other Suns?"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the Sun about to do?
options: Set the marshes on fire
Punish the Frogs for croaking
Take to himself a wife
Leave the sky forever

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do the Frogs react to the news?
options: They raise their voices to the skies in terror
They celebrate with loud songs
They hide silently beneath the water
They ask the Sun for a wedding gift

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who is disturbed by the noise the Frogs make?
options: The Sun himself
A nearby farmer
The Moon
Jupiter

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Jupiter ask the Frogs?
options: Why they live in marshes
What they were croaking about
Whether they support the marriage
How long they have lived there

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sun already do to the Frogs' home, even while single?
options: Floods their marshes with rain
Freezes their marshes overnight
Dries up their marshes with his heat
Fills their marshes with fish

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Frogs fear will happen if the Sun marries?
options: He might beget other Suns
He might grow twice as hot alone
He might abandon the sky entirely
He might move closer to the marshes

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why do the Frogs consider the Sun's marriage such alarming news?
options: They believe the Sun will forget about them once he is married
They think a wife will make the Sun kinder to them
They fear the wedding celebration will disturb their marshes
More suns like him would multiply the very harm he already causes them

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Frogs' outcry to Jupiter suggest about how they view their own situation?
options: They believe Jupiter caused the Sun's decision to marry
They see themselves as already suffering, with worse to come from something out of their control
They think the marriage will have no effect on them at all
They are indifferent to the Sun's actions in general

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "begets" mean in "if he marries and begets other Suns"?
options: Travels far away
Grows brighter
Produces offspring
Argues loudly

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: An event that seems small to others can threaten to make an existing hardship far worse
Marriages between powerful figures should always be celebrated
Jupiter is indifferent to the suffering of small creatures
The Sun's heat is not actually harmful to the marshes

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where do the Frogs raise their voices?
options: Across the marshes
Toward the Sun directly
Into the depths of the water
To the skies

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what word describes how the Frogs feel when they hear the news?
options: Joy
Terror
Curiosity
Indifference

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Frogs call the Sun's current effect on their home?
options: Barely noticeable most days
Something they have grown used to
Bad enough even while he is single
Something only other animals mind

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why do the Frogs address their complaint to Jupiter rather than to the Sun directly?
options: Jupiter is the one who notices their noise and asks them to explain it
The Sun has already refused to listen to them once before
Jupiter is known to control the Sun's marriage plans
The Frogs believe only Jupiter can grant them rain

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what assumption underlies the Frogs' fear about "other Suns"?
options: That the Sun's children would be kinder than he is
That new suns would appear only at night
That new suns would live far away from their marshes
That any offspring of the Sun would share his harmful heat

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "croaking" refer to in Jupiter's question?
options: A type of dance the Frogs performed
The sound the Frogs were making
A ritual complaint filed in writing
A song sung only at weddings

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Frogs ask Jupiter to arrange a marriage for the Sun
Frogs celebrate the Sun's wedding with the rest of the sky
Frogs cry out to Jupiter, fearing that the Sun's marriage will multiply the harm he already causes them
Jupiter punishes the Frogs for complaining about the Sun
